claim: Daughter cell positions can be specified via orienting the cell division axis during cytokinesis.
source: Daughter cell positions can be specified via orienting the cell division axis during cytokinesis.
evidence: Draws from established scientific understanding of cell division

claim: Chiral counter-rotating flows arise systematically in early AB lineage cell divisions.
source: We followed the first nine divisions of Caenorhabditis elegans embryo development and demonstrate that chiral counter-rotating flows arise systematically in early AB lineage, but not in early P/EMS lineage cell divisions.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript

claim: Chiral counter-rotating flows do not arise in early P/EMS lineage cell divisions.
source: We followed the first nine divisions of Caenorhabditis elegans embryo development and demonstrate that chiral counter-rotating flows arise systematically in early AB lineage, but not in early P/EMS lineage cell divisions.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations described in the manuscript

claim: Chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows drive lineage-specific spindle skew and cell reorientation events.
source: Combining our experiments with thin film active chiral fluid theory we identify a mechanism by which chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows arise in the AB lineage only, and show that they drive lineage-specific spindle skew and cell reorientation events.
evidence: Supported by combination of experimental data and theoretical modeling

claim: Cell positions can be specified via migration.
source: One way to achieve proper cell positioning is via migration (Scarpa and Mayor, 2016; De Pascalis and Etienne-Manneville, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The orientation of the mitotic spindle dictates the cell division axis.
source: Since the orientation of the mitotic spindle dictates the cell division axis, the orientation of the mitotic spindle at cleavage plays a key role in determining daughter cell positions (Haydar et al., 2003; Egger et al., 2007; Kulukian and Fuchs, 2013; Howard and Garzon-Coral, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The cell division axis can be set at the beginning of cytokinesis by assembling the mitotic spindle in the correct orientation from the start.
source: This axis can be set at the beginning of cytokinesis, by assembling the mitotic spindle in the correct orientation from the start, or during cytokinesis by reorientation of the mitotic spindle (Wilson, 1925; Meshcheryakov and Beloussov, 1975; Kaltschmidt et al., 2000; Matsumura et al., 2012; Sugioka and Bowerman, 2018; Galli and van den Heuvel, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The cell division axis can be set during cytokinesis by reorientation of the mitotic spindle.
source: This axis can be set at the beginning of cytokinesis, by assembling the mitotic spindle in the correct orientation from the start, or during cytokinesis by reorientation of the mitotic spindle (Wilson, 1925; Meshcheryakov and Beloussov, 1975; Kaltschmidt et al., 2000; Matsumura et al., 2012; Sugioka and Bowerman, 2018; Galli and van den Heuvel, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The mechanisms controlling reorientation of the mitotic spindle remain not very well understood.
source: While several studies highlight the mechanisms that determine the initial orientation of the mitotic spindle at the onset of cytokinesis (Sugioka and Bowerman, 2018; Matsumura et al., 2012; Kaltschmidt et al., 2000; Grill et al., 2001; Knoblich, 2010) the mechanisms controlling reorientation remain not very well understood.
evidence: Represents a gap in current scientific knowledge based on literature review

claim: The fully grown hermaphrodite C. elegans worm consists of exactly 959 somatic cells.
source: The fully grown hermaphrodite worm consists of exactly 959 somatic cells that are essentially invariant both in terms of position and lineage (Sulston and Horvitz, 1977; Sulston et al., 1983; Schnabel et al., 2006; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: C. elegans somatic cells are essentially invariant both in terms of position and lineage.
source: The fully grown hermaphrodite worm consists of exactly 959 somatic cells that are essentially invariant both in terms of position and lineage (Sulston and Horvitz, 1977; Sulston et al., 1983; Schnabel et al., 2006; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: C. elegans development is deterministic from the start.
source: Development is deterministic from the start: the one-cell embryo undergoes an asymmetric cell division that gives rise to the AB (somatic) lineage and the P lineage (Sulston et al., 1983; Bruce et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The one-cell C. elegans embryo undergoes an asymmetric cell division that gives rise to the AB (somatic) lineage and the P lineage.
source: Development is deterministic from the start: the one-cell embryo undergoes an asymmetric cell division that gives rise to the AB (somatic) lineage and the P lineage (Sulston et al., 1983; Bruce et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The anterior daughter cell AB undergoes a symmetric cell division into ABa and ABp.
source: While the anterior daughter cell, AB, undergoes a symmetric cell division into ABa and ABp, the posterior daughter cell, P1, divides asymmetrically into EMS forming the endoderm and mesoderm, and P2 forming the germ line (Sulston et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The posterior daughter cell P1 divides asymmetrically into EMS forming the endoderm and mesoderm, and P2 forming the germ line.
source: While the anterior daughter cell, AB, undergoes a symmetric cell division into ABa and ABp, the posterior daughter cell, P1, divides asymmetrically into EMS forming the endoderm and mesoderm, and P2 forming the germ line (Sulston et al., 1983).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Appropriate cell-cell contacts are instrumental for development as they can determine cell identity.
source: Appropriate cell-cell contacts are instrumental for development as they can determine cell identity (Priess, 2005; Artavanis-Tsakonas et al., 1999; Mango et al., 1994; Mello et al., 1994; Moskowitz et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Reorientation of the ABa and ABp cells via pushing with a micro needle leads to an altered cell-cell contact pattern and an altered body plan with an inverted L/R body axis.
source: For example, reorientation of the ABa and ABp cells via pushing with a micro needle leads to an altered cell-cell contact pattern and an altered body plan with an inverted L/R body axis (Wood, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: A role for the actomyosin cell cortex in determining the cell division axis of early C. elegans blastomeres was identified.
source: Recently, a role for the actomyosin cell cortex in determining the cell division axis of early C. elegans blastomeres was identified (Naganathan et al., 2014; Sugioka and Bowerman, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The actomyosin cortex is a thin layer below the plasma membrane that consists mainly of actin filaments, actin binding proteins and myosin motor proteins.
source: The actomyosin cortex is a thin layer below the plasma membrane that consists mainly of actin filaments, actin binding proteins and myosin motor proteins (Pollard and Cooper, 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Cell-cell contacts can impact on the activity of myosin and the generation of contractile stresses.
source: Cell-cell contacts can impact on the activity of myosin and the generation of contractile stresses, and the resultant pattern of cortical flows can determine the orientation of the mitotic spindle at the onset of cytokinesis (Sugioka and Bowerman, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The resultant pattern of cortical flows can determine the orientation of the mitotic spindle at the onset of cytokinesis.
source: Cell-cell contacts can impact on the activity of myosin and the generation of contractile stresses, and the resultant pattern of cortical flows can determine the orientation of the mitotic spindle at the onset of cytokinesis (Sugioka and Bowerman, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The actomyosin cortex can be thought of as a thin layer of a mechanically active fluid.
source: From a physical point of view, the actomyosin cortex can be thought of as a thin layer of a mechanically active fluid (Jülicher et al., 2007; Ramaswamy and Simha, 2006; Salbreux et al., 2009; Mayer et al., 2010) with myosin-driven active stress gradients generating cortical flows (Mayer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Myosin-driven active stress gradients generate cortical flows.
source: From a physical point of view, the actomyosin cortex can be thought of as a thin layer of a mechanically active fluid (Jülicher et al., 2007; Ramaswamy and Simha, 2006; Salbreux et al., 2009; Mayer et al., 2010) with myosin-driven active stress gradients generating cortical flows (Mayer et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Chiral rotatory cortical flows reorient the ABa cell and the ABp cell during cytokinesis, driving a cell skew of ∼20° during division.
source: These chiral rotatory cortical flows reorient the ABa cell and the ABp cell during cytokinesis, driving a cell skew of ∼20° during division (Naganathan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The cell skew results in a L/R asymmetric cell-cell contact pattern, thus executing left-right (L/R) symmetry breaking in the entire organism.
source: This skew results in a L/R asymmetric cell-cell contact pattern (Pohl and Bao, 2010), thus executing left-right (L/R) symmetry breaking in the entire organism.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and logical inference

claim: Attaching embryos to an agarose pad compresses the embryos and leads to an aspect ratio of 1.29 ± 0.14.
source: As reported before (Walston and Hardin, 2010), we found that the first method indeed compressed the embryos and leads to an aspect ratio of 1.29 ± 0.14.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements in the study

claim: Embedding embryos in low-melt agarose results in an aspect ratio of 1.02 ± 0.3 and hence a reduced compression.
source: Embedding embryos in low-melt agarose resulted in an aspect ratio of 1.02 ± 0.3 and hence a reduced compression.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements in the study

claim: Measurements of early embryos in the adult uterus revealed an aspect ratio of 1.16 ± 0.7.
source: Measurements of early embryos in the adult uterus revealed an aspect ratio of 1.16 ± 0.7. (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that in-utero embryo compression strength is intermediate.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: In-utero embryo compression strength is intermediate.
source: Measurements of early embryos in the adult uterus revealed an aspect ratio of 1.16 ± 0.7. (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), indicating that in-utero embryo compression strength is intermediate.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of aspect ratios measured under different conditions

claim: Y-direction flows in both ROIs of the P0 cell occur with the same orientation.
source: Strikingly, while y-direction flows in both ROIs of the P0 cell occur with the same orientation (Figure 1A, left), they have opposite orientations in AB cells (Figure 1A, right), such that the two dividing cell halves of the AB cell effectively spin in opposite directions.
evidence: Supported by flow measurements shown in Figure 1A

claim: Y-direction flows in AB cells have opposite orientations in the two ROIs, such that the two dividing cell halves of the AB cell effectively spin in opposite directions.
source: Strikingly, while y-direction flows in both ROIs of the P0 cell occur with the same orientation (Figure 1A, left), they have opposite orientations in AB cells (Figure 1A, right), such that the two dividing cell halves of the AB cell effectively spin in opposite directions.
evidence: Supported by flow measurements shown in Figure 1A

claim: For the AB cell division, the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity vc = −7.01 ± 0.34 µm/min.
source: For the AB cell division, we then find vc = −7.01 ± 0.34 µm/min (mean ± error of the mean at 95% confidence, unless otherwise stated), indeed indicating the presence of counter-rotating flows with consistent handedness.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: For the division of the P0 cell, counter-rotating flows are essentially absent (vc = 0.01 ± 0.51 µm/min).
source: Furthermore, for the division of the P0 cell, we find that counter-rotating flows are essentially absent (vc = 0.01 ± 0.51 µm/min).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: The cortical flows of dividing P0 cells, where both cell halves move in the same direction, correspond to net-rotating flows that resemble whole embryo rotations.
source: Instead, the cortical flows of dividing P0 cells, where both cell halves move in the same direction, correspond to net-rotating flows that resemble whole embryo rotations (Schonegg et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and citation to published literature

claim: ABa cells exhibit chiral counter-rotating flows with vc = −3.46 ± 0.33 µm/min.
source: We found that cells of the AB lineage (ABa, ABp, ABar and ABpr) exhibit chiral counter-rotating flows with vc = −3.46 ± 0.33 µm/min, −3.68 ± 0.41 µm/min, −1.24 ± 0.19 µm/min and −1.16 ± 0.22 µm/min respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B

claim: ABp cells exhibit chiral counter-rotating flows with vc = −3.68 ± 0.41 µm/min.
source: We found that cells of the AB lineage (ABa, ABp, ABar and ABpr) exhibit chiral counter-rotating flows with vc = −3.46 ± 0.33 µm/min, −3.68 ± 0.41 µm/min, −1.24 ± 0.19 µm/min and −1.16 ± 0.22 µm/min respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B

claim: ABar cells exhibit chiral counter-rotating flows with vc = −1.24 ± 0.19 µm/min.
source: We found that cells of the AB lineage (ABa, ABp, ABar and ABpr) exhibit chiral counter-rotating flows with vc = −3.46 ± 0.33 µm/min, −3.68 ± 0.41 µm/min, −1.24 ± 0.19 µm/min and −1.16 ± 0.22 µm/min respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B

claim: ABpr cells exhibit chiral counter-rotating flows with vc = −1.16 ± 0.22 µm/min.
source: We found that cells of the AB lineage (ABa, ABp, ABar and ABpr) exhibit chiral counter-rotating flows with vc = −3.46 ± 0.33 µm/min, −3.68 ± 0.41 µm/min, −1.24 ± 0.19 µm/min and −1.16 ± 0.22 µm/min respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B

claim: Average chiral counter-rotating flow velocities of P1 cells are 0.15 ±0.38 µm/min.
source: In contrast, average chiral counter-rotating flow velocities of cells of the P/EMS lineage (P1, EMS and P2) are small: 0.15 ±0.38 µm/min, 0.03 ± 0.14 µm/min and 0.25 ± 0.19 µm/min, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B

claim: Average chiral counter-rotating flow velocities of EMS cells are 0.03 ± 0.14 µm/min.
source: In contrast, average chiral counter-rotating flow velocities of cells of the P/EMS lineage (P1, EMS and P2) are small: 0.15 ±0.38 µm/min, 0.03 ± 0.14 µm/min and 0.25 ± 0.19 µm/min, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B

claim: Average chiral counter-rotating flow velocities of P2 cells are 0.25 ± 0.19 µm/min.
source: In contrast, average chiral counter-rotating flow velocities of cells of the P/EMS lineage (P1, EMS and P2) are small: 0.15 ±0.38 µm/min, 0.03 ± 0.14 µm/min and 0.25 ± 0.19 µm/min, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1B

claim: Cells of the P/EMS lineage exhibit net-rotating flows, where the y-direction flows have the same orientation in both cell halves.
source: Like P0, cells of the P/EMS lineage, instead exhibit net-rotating flows, where the y-direction flows have the same orientation in both cell halves (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, Videos 1–5).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Videos 1–5

claim: The chiral counter-rotating flow velocity vc in the AB lineage decreases as development progresses and cells become smaller.
source: We note that due to a decrease in the overall cortical flow speed, also the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity vc in the AB lineage decreases as development progresses and cells become smaller (Figure 2B, Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: The decrease in chiral counter-rotating flow velocity is accompanied by a decrease in the myosin concentration in the cytokinetic ring.
source: This is accompanied by a decrease in the myosin concentration in the cytokinetic ring (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) and is consistent with overall contractility being reduced when development progresses.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5

claim: Overall contractility is reduced when development progresses.
source: This is accompanied by a decrease in the myosin concentration in the cytokinetic ring (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) and is consistent with overall contractility being reduced when development progresses.
evidence: Inferred from the observed decrease in myosin concentration

claim: Both the presence and the strength of chiral counter-rotating flows are related to the fate of the dividing cell.
source: Together, these findings show that both the presence and the strength of chiral counter-rotating flows are related to the fate of the dividing cell.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of flows observed across different cell lineages

claim: Chiral counter-rotating flows are driven by active torque generation that depends on the myosin distribution.
source: We have shown previously that chiral counter-rotating cortical flows are driven by active torque generation that depends on the myosin distribution (Naganathan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Myosin distributions during division of the AB and the P/EMS-lineage cells differ in specific features.
source: Given that chiral counter-rotating flows arise only during AB and not P/EMS cell divisions, we hypothesize that myosin distributions during division of the AB and the P/EMS-lineage cells differ in specific features.
evidence: Hypothesis based on observed differences in flow patterns

claim: Myosin ratios in dividing AB, ABa and ABp cells are 1.0 ± 0.13, 0.92 ± 0.29, and 1.00 ± 0.24, respectively.
source: We find that myosin ratios in dividing AB, ABa and ABp cells are 1.0 ± 0.13, 0.92 ± 0.29, and 1.00 ± 0.24, respectively, indicating that there is no significant difference in cortical myosin concentration between the two halves of dividing cells from the AP lineage.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: There is no significant difference in cortical myosin concentration between the two halves of dividing cells from the AB lineage.
source: We find that myosin ratios in dividing AB, ABa and ABp cells are 1.0 ± 0.13, 0.92 ± 0.29, and 1.00 ± 0.24, respectively, indicating that there is no significant difference in cortical myosin concentration between the two halves of dividing cells from the AP lineage.
evidence: Inferred from the measured myosin ratios close to 1

claim: The myosin ratios in P0, P1 and EMS are 1.67 ± 0.3, 2.07 ± 0.61, 1.68 ± 0.33, respectively.
source: In contrast, the myosin ratios in P0, P1 and EMS are 1.67 ± 0.3, 2.07 ± 0.61, 1.68 ± 0.33, respectively (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1E

claim: The relative position of myosin peaks along the long axis of dividing AB, ABa and ABp cells are 0.49 ± 0.01, 0.49 ± 0.01 and 0.51 ± 0.02, respectively.
source: Furthermore, we find that the relative position of myosin peaks along the long axis of dividing AB, ABa and ABp cells are 0.49 ± 0.01, 0.49 ± 0.01 and 0.51 ± 0.02, respectively.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: Myosin peaks in dividing P0, P1 and EMS cells are positioned at 0.58 ± 0.01, 0.57 ± 0.02 and 0.59 ± 0.01 relative to cell length, respectively.
source: In contrast, myosin peaks in dividing P0, P1 and EMS cells are positioned at 0.58 ± 0.01, 0.57 ± 0.02 and 0.59 ± 0.01 relative to cell length, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1D

claim: The early cell divisions of the AB lineage are symmetric in terms of myosin intensity ratio and cytokinetic ring position.
source: To conclude, the early cell divisions of the AB lineage are symmetric in terms of myosin intensity ratio and cytokinetic ring position, while early cell divisions of the P/EMS lineage are asymmetric in these two features.
evidence: Inferred from the measured myosin ratios and ring positions

claim: Early cell divisions of the P/EMS lineage are asymmetric in terms of myosin intensity ratio and cytokinetic ring position.
source: To conclude, the early cell divisions of the AB lineage are symmetric in terms of myosin intensity ratio and cytokinetic ring position, while early cell divisions of the P/EMS lineage are asymmetric in these two features.
evidence: Inferred from the measured myosin ratios and ring positions

claim: A symmetric myosin distribution and cytokinetic ring position result in a maximum value of vc.
source: We find that a symmetric myosin distribution and cytokinetic ring position (myosin ratio ≈1, relative myosin peak position ≈0.5) result in a maximum value of vc.
evidence: Supported by theoretical modeling using thin film active chiral fluid theory

claim: Myosin ratios different from one and an asymmetric ring position result in smaller values of vc.
source: Accordingly, myosin ratios different from one and an asymmetric ring position result in smaller values of vc, where the model suggests that vc is more sensitive to changes in the myosin ratio than to changes in the ring position (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7

claim: vc is more sensitive to changes in the myosin ratio than to changes in the ring position.
source: Accordingly, myosin ratios different from one and an asymmetric ring position result in smaller values of vc, where the model suggests that vc is more sensitive to changes in the myosin ratio than to changes in the ring position (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Supported by theoretical modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7

claim: The switch between chiral and non-chiral flows between the two lineages could in principle be attributed to the observed difference in myosin ratio, cytokinetic ring position or both.
source: Our results indicate that the switch between chiral and non-chiral flows between the two lineages could in principle be attributed to the observed difference in myosin ratio, cytokinetic ring position or both (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Inferred from theoretical modeling and experimental observations

claim: The thin film active chiral fluid theory can quantitatively relate y-direction flows of dividing AB, ABa, and ABp cells with the myosin profiles along their long axis.
source: We note, however, that while the thin film active chiral fluid theory can quantitatively relate y-direction flows of dividing AB, ABa, and ABp cells with the myosin profiles along their long axis (Figure 1—figure supplement 8, Appendix 1—table 1), this is not possible for the P/EMS lineage.
evidence: Supported by theoretical modeling and comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8

claim: The thin film active chiral fluid theory cannot quantitatively relate y-direction flows with myosin profiles for the P/EMS lineage.
source: We note, however, that while the thin film active chiral fluid theory can quantitatively relate y-direction flows of dividing AB, ABa, and ABp cells with the myosin profiles along their long axis (Figure 1—figure supplement 8, Appendix 1—table 1), this is not possible for the P/EMS lineage.
evidence: Limitation of the theoretical model when applied to P/EMS lineage

claim: The understanding of the mechanisms that lead to the cortical flows in P/EMS linage divisions is still incomplete.
source: This indicates that our understanding of the mechanisms that lead to the cortical flows in P/EMS linage divisions is still incomplete.
evidence: Inferred from the inability of the theoretical model to explain P/EMS flows

claim: The occurrence of chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows depends on the amount of cortical myosin in the cell halves and the position of the cytokinetic ring.
source: Taken together, our analysis implies a mechanism whereby the occurrence of chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows depends on the amount of cortical myosin in the cell halves and the position of the cytokinetic ring.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and theoretical modeling

claim: The first cell division in wild-type embryos is asymmetric and does not display chiral counter-rotating flows.
source: The first cell division in wild-type embryos is asymmetric and does not display chiral counter-rotating flows.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The asymmetry of the P0 division is controlled by Par polarity complexes.
source: The asymmetry of the P0 division is controlled by Par polarity complexes (Kemphues et al., 1988) and depletion of the posterior Par protein, PAR-2, led to a symmetric myosin distribution with a myosin ratio of one and centered ring position (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature and experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9

claim: Depletion of PAR-2 led to a symmetric myosin distribution with a myosin ratio of one and centered ring position.
source: The asymmetry of the P0 division is controlled by Par polarity complexes (Kemphues et al., 1988) and depletion of the posterior Par protein, PAR-2, led to a symmetric myosin distribution with a myosin ratio of one and centered ring position (Figure 1—figure supplement 9).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9

claim: par-2 depletion triggered the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flow during P0 cytokinesis (vc = −5.71 ± 0.89 µm/min).
source: Strikingly, par-2 depletion also triggered the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flow during P0 cytokinesis (vc = −5.71 ± 0.89 µm/min; Figure 1—figure supplement 9) demonstrating that inducing symmetric cell division via par-2 (RNAi) is sufficient to trigger chiral counter-rotating flows in P0.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 9

claim: Inducing symmetric cell division via par-2 (RNAi) is sufficient to trigger chiral counter-rotating flows in P0.
source: Strikingly, par-2 depletion also triggered the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flow during P0 cytokinesis (vc = −5.71 ± 0.89 µm/min; Figure 1—figure supplement 9) demonstrating that inducing symmetric cell division via par-2 (RNAi) is sufficient to trigger chiral counter-rotating flows in P0.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental observation that par-2 depletion causes both symmetric division and chiral flows

claim: A centered ring position should result in chiral counter-rotating flows regardless of myosin asymmetry.
source: Moreover, our hydrodynamic theory predicts that a centered ring position should result in chiral counter-rotating flows regardless of myosin asymmetry (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: Prediction from theoretical modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7

claim: LIN-5 is involved in generating asymmetric pulling forces that displace the spindle from the center.
source: LIN-5 is involved in generating asymmetric pulling forces that displace the spindle from the center (Galli and van den Heuvel, 2008; Lorson et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The myosin distribution in P0 is still asymmetric in lin-5 (RNAi) embryos, while the ring position is at the center.
source: We first confirmed that indeed the myosin distribution in P0 is still asymmetric in these embryos (albeit reduced when compared with control), while the ring position is at the center (Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 10

claim: lin-5 (RNAi) triggered the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flows (vc = −1.73 ± 0.74 µm/min).
source: Quantifying cortical actomyosin flows revealed that lin-5 (RNAi) triggered the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flows (vc = −1.73 ± 0.74 µm/min; Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 10

claim: The emergence of chiral counter-rotating flows upon lin-5 (RNAi) is unlikely to be the result of higher overall actomyosin activity.
source: Given that cortical myosin levels upon lin-5 (RNAi) are comparable to those observed in control, the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flows is unlikely to be the result of higher overall actomyosin activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 10).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of myosin levels shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 10

claim: Both asymmetries in myosin distribution and ring position counteract the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flows.
source: Although we cannot fully uncouple the effect of myosin asymmetry and ring position, these experimental results are qualitatively consistent with our theoretical predictions and thus suggest that both, asymmetries in myosin distribution and ring position, counteract the emergence of chiral counter-rotating flows.
evidence: Inferred from experimental results and theoretical predictions

claim: Symmetric cell division is required for chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows to emerge during cytokinesis.
source: We conclude that symmetric cell division is required for chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows to emerge during cytokinesis.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with par-2 and lin-5 perturbations

claim: Specific rotations of the spindle (termed spindle skews) are thought to be a key mechanism by which dividing cells reposition themselves in the embryo.
source: Specific rotations of the spindle (termed spindle skews) are thought to be a key mechanism by which dividing cells reposition themselves in the embryo (Naganathan et al., 2014; Singh and Pohl, 2014; Liro and Rose, 2016; Bergmann et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Cells of the early AB lineage undergo an average skew angle of 21.17 ± 3.22°.
source: We find that cells of the early AB lineage undergo an average skew angle of 21.17 ± 3.22° (AB: 37.51 ± 2.51°, ABa: 27.64 ± 2.29°, ABp: 23.98 ± 1.19°, ABal: 17.73 ± 1.98°, ABar: 15.51 ± 3.51°, ABpl: 10.43 ± 1.92° and ABpr: 15.42 ± 2.11°).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: P/EMS lineage cells undergo significantly reduced spindle skews with an average skew angle of 2.32 ± 0.43°.
source: In comparison, P/EMS lineage cells undergo significantly reduced spindle skews with an average skew angle of of 2.32 ± 0.43° (P0: 2.31 ± 1.67°, P1: 2.25 ± 0.66°, EMS: 2.66 ± 1.25°, P2: 4.36 ± 1.67°).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: Spindle skew angles in the AB lineage decrease as development progresses.
source: Note also, that spindle skew angles in the AB lineage decrease as development progresses, while the P/EMS lineage spindle skew angles remain small and approximately constant (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B

claim: P/EMS lineage spindle skew angles remain small and approximately constant as development progresses.
source: Note also, that spindle skew angles in the AB lineage decrease as development progresses, while the P/EMS lineage spindle skew angles remain small and approximately constant (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 2B

claim: Cells that exhibit significant chiral counter-rotating flows also undergo significant spindle skews during early development.
source: Given that AB lineage cells, but not P/EMS lineage cells, undergo chiral counter-rotating flows, we conclude that cells that exhibit significant chiral counter-rotating flows also undergo significant spindle skews during early development (Figure 2B).
evidence: Inferred from correlation between flow patterns and spindle skews shown in Figure 2B

claim: The skew of the ABa and ABp cells is a three-dimensional process, tilting the spindle in both the anteroposterior-left-right (AP-LR) plane and in the orthogonal left-right-dorsoventral (LR-DV) plane.
source: In our earlier work, we showed that the skew of the ABa and ABp cells is in fact a three-dimensional process, tilting the spindle in both the anteroposterior-left-right (AP-LR) plane and in the orthogonal left-right-dorsoventral (LR-DV) plane (Naganathan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The spindle skew in the AB cell in the AP-DV plane is similar in compressed and uncompressed conditions (37.51 ± 2.51° and 36.67 ± 9.24°, respectively).
source: Chiral counter-rotating flows in the AB cell could still be observed and the spindle skew in the AP-DV plane was similar in compressed and uncompressed conditions (37.51 ± 2.51° and 36.67 ± 9.24°, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements

claim: The absence of embryo compression revealed a significant clockwise skew in the LR-DV plane with a skew angle of 31.85 ± 11.11° when viewed from the anterior.
source: However, the absence of embryo compression revealed a significant clockwise skew in the LR-DV plane (when viewed from the anterior) with a skew angle of 31.85 ± 11.11° (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Video 10).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: No significant skew was observed in the P1 cell in the LR-DV plane.
source: We did not observe any significant skew in the P1 cell in the LR-DV plane (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Skews of the AB cell division axis are a three-dimensional process, where the skew occurs in both the AP-DV and LR-DV planes.
source: These findings show that skews of the AB cell division axis are in fact also a three-dimensional process, where the skew occurs in both the AP-DV and LR-DV planes.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations of skews in both planes

claim: Anteriorizing the embryo via par-2; chin-1; lgl-1 (RNAi) results in the second and the third cell division exhibiting chiral counter-rotating flows with vc values that are not significantly different from one another (−6.53 ± 1.13 µm/min and −6.67 ± 0.8 µm/min, respectively).
source: Consistent with the first expectation, anteriorizing the embryo via par-2; chin-1; lgl-1 (RNAi) (Beatty et al., 2013) results in the second and the third cell division exhibiting chiral counter-rotating flows with vc values that are not significantly different from one another (−6.53 ± 1.13 µm/min and −6.67 ± 0.8 µm/min, respectively; Wilcoxon rank sum test at 95% confidence; Figure 3B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3B,C

claim: Posteriorizing the embryo via par-6 (RNAi) results in both the second and the third cell division not exhibiting counter-rotating flows (vc = 0.07 ± 0.71 µm/min and −0.85 ± 1.13 µm/min, respectively).
source: Consistent with the second expectation, posteriorizing the embryo via par-6 (RNAi) (Hung and Kemphues, 1999) results in both the second and the third cell division not exhibiting counter-rotating flows (vc = 0.07 ± 0.71 µm/min and −0.85 ± 1.13 µm/min, respectively; Figure 3B,C, Videos 11–13).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3B,C and Videos 11–13

claim: Cell fate determines the presence or absence of chiral counter-rotating flows.
source: Hence, cell fate determines the presence or absence of chiral counter-rotating flows.
evidence: Inferred from experiments with anteriorizing and posteriorizing perturbations

claim: Switching the cell fate results in concomitant changes in the spindle skew angle in the AP-DV plane for both the second and third cell division in compressed as well as non-compressed embryos.
source: Furthermore, switching the cell fate results in concomitant changes in the spindle skew angle in the AP-DV plane for both the second and third cell division in compressed as well as non-compressed embryos (Figure 3D,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3D,H

claim: Spindles of the two AB-like cells in uncompressed anteriorized embryos undergo clockwise skew in the LR-DV plane when viewed from the closest pole (skew angles of each AB-like cell = 26.93 ± 6.78° and 27.44 ± 8.66°).
source: Strikingly, we observed that spindles of the two AB-like cells in uncompressed anteriorized embryos undergo clockwise skew in the LR-DV plane when viewed from the closest pole (skew angles of each AB-like cell = 26.93 ± 6.78° and 27.44 ± 8.66°) (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Videos 14–16).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: Cell fate determines both the presence of chiral counter-rotating flows and the degree as well as the direction of spindle skew.
source: We conclude that cell fate determines both the presence of chiral counter-rotating flows and the degree as well as the direction of spindle skew.
evidence: Inferred from experiments with cell fate perturbations

claim: Weak perturbation RNAi of ect-2 results in vc = −3.57 ± 0.57 µm/min, which is reduced in comparison to the unperturbed embryo (vc = −6.6 ± 0.37 µm/min).
source: Weak perturbation RNAi of ect-2 results in vc = −3.57 ± 0.57 µm/min, which is reduced in comparison to the unperturbed embryo (vc = −6.6 ± 0.37 µm/min, Wilcoxon rank sum test at 95% confidence, Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: Weak perturbation RNAi of rga-3 increases the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity to vc = −8.71 ± 0.58 µm/min.
source: Conversely, weak perturbation RNAi of rga-3 increases the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity to vc = −8.71 ± 0.58 µm/min (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4A,B

claim: ect-2 and rga-3 perturbations impact only chiral counter-rotating flows, and do not significantly change overall contractility.
source: Note that these perturbations impact only chiral counter-rotating flows, and do not significantly change overall contractility, as illustrated by the on-axis flow into the contractile ring, which is not significantly altered (Wilcoxon rank sum test at 95% confidence, Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4C

claim: Decreasing the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity by mild ect-2 (RNAi) leads to concomitant reduction of the rate of spindle skew (average peak rate: 0.59 ± 0.05°/min) as compared to 1.01 ± 0.1°/min in control embryos.
source: We indeed find that decreasing the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity by mild ect-2 (RNAi) leads to concomitant reduction of the rate of spindle skew (average peak rate: 0.59 ± 0.05°/min, Video 17) as compared to 1.01 ± 0.1°/min in control embryos (Figure 4D, Video 18).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4D

claim: Increasing RhoA signaling by mild rga-3 (RNAi) treatment leads to an increase of both the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity and the rate of spindle skew (average peak rate: 1.29 ± 0.12°/min).
source: Conversely, increasing RhoA signaling by mild rga-3 (RNAi) treatment leads to an increase of both the chiral counter-rotating flow velocity and the rate of spindle skew (average peak rate: 1.29 ± 0.12°/min (Video 19, Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4D

claim: The peak rates of spindle elongation remain unchanged as compared to the control for both ect-2 and rga-3 perturbations.
source: Note that the peak rates of spindle elongation remain unchanged as compared to the control for both perturbations (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Changing chiral counter-rotating flow velocities results in concomitant changes of the rates of spindle skews without impacting on the dynamics of spindle elongation.
source: We conclude that changing chiral counter-rotating flow velocities results in concomitant changes of the rates of spindle skews without impacting on the dynamics of spindle elongation.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with ect-2 and rga-3 perturbations

claim: Overall actomyosin contractility is unlikely to contribute significantly to cell division skews.
source: In addition, given that the contractility-driven flows remain unaltered upon rga-3 (RNAi) and ect-2 (RNAi), overall actomyosin contractility is unlikely to contribute significantly to cell division skews.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that contractile flows are unchanged while skew rates change

claim: Chiral counter-rotating flows mechanically drive cell skews and consequently also spindle skews.
source: These results instead support our second hypothesis, that chiral counter-rotating flows mechanically drive cell skews and consequently also spindle skews.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations showing correlation between flow velocities and skew rates

claim: The AB cell exhibits chiral counter-rotating flows during division (vc = −5.05 ± 1.12 µm/min) upon lin-5 depletion.
source: Moreover, the AB cell exhibited chiral counter-rotating flows during division (vc = −5.05 ± 1.12 µm/min) and, although the AB spindle was often misaligned, it skewed substantially during anaphase (spindle skew angle = 23.14 ± 7.46°, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The AB spindle skewed substantially during anaphase upon lin-5 depletion (spindle skew angle = 23.14 ± 7.46°).
source: Moreover, the AB cell exhibited chiral counter-rotating flows during division (vc = −5.05 ± 1.12 µm/min) and, although the AB spindle was often misaligned, it skewed substantially during anaphase (spindle skew angle = 23.14 ± 7.46°, Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The known spindle orientation pathway does not play an important role in driving spindle skews.
source: These results argue against an important role for the known spindle orientation pathway in driving spindle skews.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with lin-5 and gpr-1/2 perturbations

claim: The LIN-5-dependent spindle orientation pathway is known to reorient the metaphase spindle in the P1 cell.
source: Alternatively, given that the LIN-5-dependent spindle orientation pathway is known to reorient the metaphase spindle in the P1 cell, this pathway might inhibit actomyosin dependent spindle skews in the P/EMS lineage during anaphase.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge

claim: Analyzing spindle skews in P1 upon lin-5 (RNAi) and gpr-1/2 (RNAi) revealed no significant difference when compared to control embryos.
source: Analyzing spindle skews in P1 upon lin-5 (RNAi) and gpr-1/2 (RNAi) revealed no significant difference when compared to control embryos, which suggests that the spindle orientation pathway does not overrule actomyosin-dependent spindle skews (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The spindle orientation pathway does not overrule actomyosin-dependent spindle skews.
source: Analyzing spindle skews in P1 upon lin-5 (RNAi) and gpr-1/2 (RNAi) revealed no significant difference when compared to control embryos, which suggests that the spindle orientation pathway does not overrule actomyosin-dependent spindle skews (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The LIN-5/GPR-1/2-dependent spindle orientation pathway determines the initial spindle orientation, while chiral actomyosin flows drive the spindle skews observed during anaphase.
source: Altogether, we conclude that the LIN-5/GPR-1/2-dependent spindle orientation pathway determines the initial spindle orientation, while chiral actomyosin flows drive the spindle skews observed during anaphase.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with lin-5 and gpr-1/2 perturbations

claim: In all nmy-2(ts) mutant embryos (12 out of 12), an ingressing cytokinetic ring was absent and cytokinesis failed after temperature shifting.
source: In all nmy-2(ts) mutant embryos (12 out of 12), an ingressing cytokinetic ring was absent and cytokinesis failed after temperature shifting, indicating that NMY-2 was effectively inactivated (Davies et al., 2014; Videos 20 and 21).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The dynamics of spindle elongation, including the peak rate of spindle elongation and the final spindle length, are essentially unchanged in nmy-2(ts) mutants as compared to control embryos at restrictive temperature.
source: Interestingly, while the dynamics of spindle elongation, including the peak rate of spindle elongation and the final spindle length, are essentially unchanged as compared to control embryos at restrictive temperature, the average peak rate of spindle skew was significantly reduced (0.33 ± 0.09°/min as compared to 1.43 ± 0.13°/min in control embryos, Wilcoxon rank sum test at 95% confidence, Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Videos 20 and 21).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: The average peak rate of spindle skew was significantly reduced in nmy-2(ts) mutants (0.33 ± 0.09°/min) as compared to 1.43 ± 0.13°/min in control embryos.
source: Interestingly, while the dynamics of spindle elongation, including the peak rate of spindle elongation and the final spindle length, are essentially unchanged as compared to control embryos at restrictive temperature, the average peak rate of spindle skew was significantly reduced (0.33 ± 0.09°/min as compared to 1.43 ± 0.13°/min in control embryos, Wilcoxon rank sum test at 95% confidence, Figure 5A,B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Videos 20 and 21).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: A functional actomyosin cortex with chiral cortical flows is required for spindle skews of the AB cell.
source: This demonstrates that a functional actomyosin cortex with chiral cortical flows is required for spindle skews of the AB cell.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with nmy-2(ts) mutants

claim: Spindle skews in the AB cell are independent of spindle elongation, but are instead a consequence of the cell skews that are driven by chiral counter-rotating flows.
source: In light of our experiments above, we conclude that spindle skews in the AB cell are independent of spindle elongation, but are instead a consequence of the cell skews that are driven by chiral counter-rotating flows.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations showing spindle elongation is unchanged while skew is reduced

claim: All cells belonging to the AB cell lineage show a significantly reduced skew in the nmy-2(ts) embryos at restrictive temperatures as compared to the control.
source: Finally, we performed temperature shift experiments for the first 11 divisions in the nematode, and found that all cells belonging to the AB cell lineage show a significantly reduced skew in the nmy-2(ts) embryos at restrictive temperatures as compared to the control (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 5C

claim: A functional actomyosin cortex with chiral cortical flows is required for spindle skews of early AB lineage cell divisions during worm development.
source: We conclude that a functional actomyosin cortex with chiral cortical flows is required for spindle skews of early AB lineage cell divisions during worm development.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations with nmy-2(ts) mutants across multiple divisions

claim: The direction of the cell division skew is determined by the handedness of the chiral counter-rotating flow and the distribution of friction forces across the cellular surface.
source: Following this analogy, the direction of the cell division skew is determined by (1) the handedness of the chiral counter-rotating flow and (2) the distribution of friction forces across the cellular surface.
evidence: Inferred from physical modeling and experimental observations

claim: The AB cell simultaneously skews in two orthogonal planes, AP-DV and LR-DV.
source: As described above, the AB cell simultaneously skews in two orthogonal planes, AP-DV and LR-DV.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations

claim: The clockwise skew in the LR-DV plane is consistent with the handedness of the chiral counter-rotating cortical flows, assuming high friction forces at the AB-P1 interface.
source: Assuming that there are high friction forces at the AB-P1 interface, the clockwise skew (when viewed from the anterior down the anteroposterior axis) in the LR-DV plane is consistent with the handedness of the chiral counter-rotating cortical flows (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Inferred from physical modeling and experimental observations

claim: For the observed clockwise skew in the AP-DV plane to be consistent with the handedness of chiral counter-rotating flows of AB, the total friction forces between the AB cell and vitelline layer and/or the egg shell are elevated on the right side of the embryo, as compared to the left side.
source: Similarly, for the observed clockwise skew in the AP-DV plane (when viewed from the left down the left-right axis) to be consistent with the handedness of chiral counter-rotating flows of AB, we expect that the total friction forces between the AB cell and vitelline layer and/or the egg shell are elevated on the right side of the embryo, as compared to the left side (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Inferred from physical modeling and experimental observations

claim: Cortical flow speeds may be different on the future left and right sides of the dividing AB cell due to left-right asymmetric friction forces.
source: Because such forces are expected to reduce cortical flow speed, we argued that cortical flow speeds may be different on the future left and right sides of the dividing AB cell.
evidence: Inferred from the expected effect of friction forces on flow speeds

claim: Y-direction flows in each cell half, and consequently vc, are significantly increased on the left side of the AB cell, as compared to the right side.
source: Measuring the chiral counter-rotating flow velocities of the AB cell also on the left side, we indeed find that y-direction flows in each cell half, and consequently vc, are significantly increased on the left side, as compared to the right side (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, velocity values are given in Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: The observation that flows are increased on the left side is consistent with the hypothesis that the friction forces experienced by the AB cell are higher on the right side than on the left side.
source: This observation is consistent with the hypothesis that the friction forces experienced by the AB cell are higher on the right side than on the left side.
evidence: Inferred from the measured flow velocities

claim: The calculated angular skew velocities agree well with the experimentally measured average AP-DV spindle skew rates of the dividing AB cell for wild type, ect-2 (RNAi) and rga-3 (RNAi) conditions.
source: We measured y-direction flows (measurement in the 'lab frame') in wild type, ect-2 (RNAi) and rga-3 (RNAi) on the left and right side of the embryo and found for all three conditions that the calculated angular skew velocities agree well with the experimentally measured average AP-DV spindle skew rates of the dividing AB cell (Appendix 1—table 3).
evidence: Supported by comparison of theoretical calculations with experimental measurements

claim: The skewing motion and chiral flows across the AB cell cortex are compatible with a simplified geometry that is analogous to a spinning bulldozer.
source: Additionally, it shows that the skewing motion and chiral flows across the AB cell cortex are compatible with a simplified geometry that is analogous to a spinning bulldozer.
evidence: Inferred from the agreement between theoretical model and experimental observations

claim: The AB cell surface area that is in contact with the egg shell is different on the left and ride side of the embryo, thus contributing to an asymmetry in the corresponding friction forces.
source: A second possibility we favor is that the AB cell surface area that is in contact with the egg shell is different on the left and ride side of the embryo, thus contributing to an asymmetry in the corresponding friction forces.
evidence: Hypothesis based on physical reasoning

claim: The cytokinetic ring of the AB cell ingresses in a left-right asymmetric fashion and pinches off toward the embryo's right side.
source: Interestingly, an earlier report showed that the cytokinetic ring of the AB cell ingresses in a left-right asymmetric fashion and pinches off toward the embryo's right side (Schonegg et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Left/right asymmetric ring ingression likely reduces the AB cell surface area that contacts the egg shell.
source: Left/right asymmetric ring ingression likely reduces the AB cell surface area that contacts the egg shell, and – given that ring ingression begins on the left side – this could lead to a left-right asymmetry in contact surface area and thus also an asymmetry in the resulting frictional forces.
evidence: Inferred from the observed asymmetric ring ingression

claim: A reduced surface area on the left side of the AB cell was measured from confocal imaging of the actomyosin cortex on left and right sides.
source: From our confocal imaging of the actomyosin cortex on left and right sides, we indeed measured a reduced surface area on the left side of the AB cell (Figure 5—figure supplement 3, Appendix 1—table 4, see Appendix).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3

claim: A physical model that incorporates the measured values yields agreement with experimentally measured cell division skews.
source: While these measurements, as well as the fits to approximate the local friction coefficients, only provide coarse approximations, a physical model that incorporates the measured values yields agreement with experimentally measured cell division skews.
evidence: Supported by comparison of theoretical model with experimental measurements

claim: Large-scale cellular rearrangements can be accounted for at a quantitative level from the interplay between chiral surface flows and spatial patterns of effective friction forces.
source: Hence, our results show that large-scale cellular rearrangements can be accounted for at a quantitative level from the interplay between chiral surface flows and spatial patterns of effective friction forces.
evidence: Inferred from the quantitative agreement between model and experiments

claim: Chiral rotatory movements of the actomyosin cortex are more prevalent in development than one might have suspected.
source: To conclude, our work shows that chiral rotatory movements of the actomyosin cortex are more prevalent in development than one might have suspected.
evidence: Inferred from the systematic observation of chiral flows across multiple cell divisions

claim: The cells of the early embryo represent a new class of active chiral material that requires an explicit treatment of angular momentum conservation.
source: This is interesting from a physical perspective, since together the cells of the early embryo represent a new class of active chiral material that requires an explicit treatment of angular momentum conservation (Fürthauer et al., 2013; Naganathan et al., 2014).
evidence: Inferred from the observed chiral flows and supported by citations to published literature

claim: Cell skews driven by actomyosin torque generation represent a novel class of lineage-specific morphogenetic rearrangements.
source: This is interesting from a biological perspective, since cell skews driven by actomyosin torque generation represent a novel class of lineage-specific morphogenetic rearrangements.
evidence: Inferred from the observed lineage-specific pattern of chiral flows and cell skews

claim: Lineage-specific chiral flows of the actomyosin cortex drive lineage-specific cell rearrangements in early C. elegans development.
source: In this work, we have shown that lineage-specific chiral flows of the actomyosin cortex drive lineage-specific cell rearrangements in early C. elegans development.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations throughout the study

claim: Actomyosin flows are required for determining the initial orientation of the mitotic spindle.
source: Recently, it was demonstrated that actomyosin flows are required for determining the initial orientation of the mitotic spindle (Sugioka and Bowerman, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The actomyosin cortex drives an active counter-rotation of the two halves of dividing early AB lineage cells, leading to cellular repositioning of these cells during anaphase.
source: Here, we have shown that the actomyosin cortex drives an active counter-rotation of the two halves of dividing early AB lineage cells, leading to cellular repositioning of these cells during anaphase.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations in the study

claim: Chiral counter-rotating flows represent a general mechanism by which dividing cells can reorient themselves in order to allow their daughters to achieve their appropriate positions.
source: We propose that chiral counter-rotating flows represent a general mechanism by which dividing cells can reorient themselves in order to allow their daughters to achieve their appropriate positions.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the observed pattern of chiral flows and cell repositioning

claim: During early C. elegans development cell lineage specifications are mainly driven by short-range intercellular signaling cascades.
source: During early C. elegans development cell lineage specifications are mainly driven by short-range intercellular signaling cascades (Priess, 2005; Eisenmann, 2005) and therefore, correct positioning of blastomeres is instrumental for normal development.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Correct positioning of blastomeres is instrumental for normal development.
source: During early C. elegans development cell lineage specifications are mainly driven by short-range intercellular signaling cascades (Priess, 2005; Eisenmann, 2005) and therefore, correct positioning of blastomeres is instrumental for normal development.
evidence: Inferred from the role of short-range signaling in cell lineage specification

claim: The cell division skew of the AB blastomere puts the ABp daughter cell in close contact with the posterior P2 cell.
source: For example, the cell division skew of the AB blastomere puts the ABp daughter cell in close contact with the posterior P2 cell.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge

claim: Close contact between ABp and P2 results in Notch signaling activation in the ABp cell but not in the ABa cell, triggering the distinct development of the ABa and ABp lineages.
source: In turn, this results in Notch signaling activation in the ABp cell but not in the ABa cell, triggering the distinct development of the ABa and ABp lineages (Hutter and Schnabel, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The subsequent spindle skew of ABa and ABp lies at the heart of left-right patterning and is essential for proper left-right asymmetric inductions.
source: The subsequent spindle skew of ABa and ABp lies at the heart of left-right patterning and is essential for proper left-right asymmetric inductions, again driven by short-range signaling cascades (Pohl and Bao, 2010; Hardin and King, 2008; Walston and Hardin, 2006; Priess, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The chiral flow-driven spindle skews allow cells in the AB lineage to acquire their precise position and thereby permit normal cell fate inductions.
source: We propose that the chiral flow-driven spindle skews described here, allow cells in the AB lineage to acquire their precise position and thereby permit normal cell fate inductions.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the observed role of chiral flows in cell positioning

claim: AB lineage cells divide symmetrically, while the early P/EMS lineage cell divisions are asymmetric.
source: We know that AB lineage cells divide symmetrically, while the early P/EMS lineage cell divisions are asymmetric (Rose and Gönczy, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: The occurrence of chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows depends on the amount of cortical myosin in each cell half and on the position of the cytokinetic ring.
source: We have shown here that the occurrence of chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows depends on the amount of cortical myosin in each cell half and on the position of the cytokinetic ring.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations in the study

claim: Cell lineage determinants like PAR proteins likely act to control chiral flows by modulating the distribution of molecular motors along the cell division axis.
source: Cell lineage determinants like PAR proteins, instrumental for cell polarity, therefore likely act to control chiral flows by modulating the distribution of molecular motors along the cell division axis (Gross et al., 2019; Munro et al., 2004) .
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and supported by citations to published literature

claim: Chiral active fluid theory can be used to describe the chiral counter-rotating flows during zygote polarization.
source: We showed previously that chiral active fluid theory can be used to describe the chiral counter-rotating flows during zygote polarization.
evidence: Supported by reference to previous work

claim: In the coarse-grained hydrodynamic description, the cortex is treated as a two-dimensional gel that has liquid-like properties and generates active torques.
source: In this coarse-grained hydrodynamic description, the cortex is treated as a two-dimensional gel that has liquid-like properties and generates active torques.
evidence: Description of the theoretical framework used

claim: Active torques tend to locally rotate the cortex clockwise (when viewed from the outside) and thereby determine flow handedness.
source: In turn, these torques tend to locally rotate the cortex clockwise (when viewed from the outside) and thereby determine flow handedness.
evidence: Description of the theoretical framework used

claim: Assuming that the local torque density is proportional to the measured NMY-2 levels, the theory can quantitatively recapitulate the observed chiral flow behavior in the dividing AB blastomeres.
source: Assuming that the local torque density is proportional to the measured NMY-2 levels, we have shown here that this theory can quantitatively recapitulate the observed chiral flow behavior in the dividing AB blastomeres (Figure 1—figure supplement 8).
evidence: Supported by theoretical modeling and comparison with experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 8

claim: The molecular underpinnings that determine the observed flow handedness remain elusive.
source: However, the molecular underpinnings that determine the observed flow handedness remain elusive.
evidence: Represents a gap in current understanding

claim: Many actin-binding proteins localize in a pattern similar to myosin.
source: Additionally, given that many actin-binding proteins localize in a pattern similar to myosin (Tse et al., 2012; Maddox et al., 2005; Motegi and Sugimoto, 2006; Davies et al., 2018), and many of these affect the chirality of actomyosin flows in the polarizing one-cell embryo (Naganathan et al., 2018), we cannot exclude that other force generators provide the active torque needed for chiral counter-rotating flows.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Many actin-binding proteins affect the chirality of actomyosin flows in the polarizing one-cell embryo.
source: Additionally, given that many actin-binding proteins localize in a pattern similar to myosin (Tse et al., 2012; Maddox et al., 2005; Motegi and Sugimoto, 2006; Davies et al., 2018), and many of these affect the chirality of actomyosin flows in the polarizing one-cell embryo (Naganathan et al., 2018), we cannot exclude that other force generators provide the active torque needed for chiral counter-rotating flows.
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature

claim: Myosins can twist actin filaments while they pull them due to the helical nature of actin.
source: Due to the helical nature of actin, both myosins (Lebreton et al., 2018) and formins (Mizuno et al., 2011; Jégou et al., 2013) can twist actin filaments while they respectively pull or polymerize them, and therefore both are potential sources of molecular torques.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Formins can twist actin filaments while they polymerize them due to the helical nature of actin.
source: Due to the helical nature of actin, both myosins (Lebreton et al., 2018) and formins (Mizuno et al., 2011; Jégou et al., 2013) can twist actin filaments while they respectively pull or polymerize them, and therefore both are potential sources of molecular torques.
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: Myosins and formins are potential sources of molecular torques.
source: Due to the helical nature of actin, both myosins (Lebreton et al., 2018) and formins (Mizuno et al., 2011; Jégou et al., 2013) can twist actin filaments while they respectively pull or polymerize them, and therefore both are potential sources of molecular torques.
evidence: Inferred from the ability of myosins and formins to twist actin filaments

claim: Myosins as well as formins are required for numerous cellular and organismal chiral processes.
source: Interestingly, myosins as well as formins are also required for numerous cellular and organismal chiral processes (Tee et al., 2015; Davison et al., 2016; Kuroda et al., 2016; Hozumi et al., 2006; Maderspacher, 2016; Spéder et al., 2006; Chougule et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature

claim: The handedness of chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows, together with asymmetries in the effective friction forces between cells and the surrounding determine the direction of cell division skews.
source: Our work shows that the handedness of chiral counter-rotating actomyosin flows, together with asymmetries in the effective friction forces between cells and the surrounding determine the direction of cell division skews (Figure 3A right panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations and theoretical modeling

claim: Chiral flow-driven cell division skews represent a three-dimensional process in which skews occur simultaneously in different planes.
source: Therefore, chiral flow-driven cell division skews represent a three-dimensional process in which skews occur simultaneously in different planes (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Obvious sources of an effective friction force between cell-cell contacts are provided by adhesions.
source: Obvious sources of an effective friction force between cell-cell contacts are provided by adhesions.
evidence: Draws from established scientific knowledge

claim: Differences in friction forces exist between the AB blastomere and the egg shell on the left and right side.
source: Moreover, our results suggest that differences in friction forces also exist between the AB blastomere and the egg shell on the left and right side.
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and theoretical modeling

claim: This friction force difference, together with the handedness of the chiral counter-rotating flow will cause the AB cell to skew clockwise in the AP-DV plane (when viewed from the left side down the left-right axis), thereby establishing the dorsoventral axis.
source: This friction force difference, together with the handedness of the chiral counter-rotating flow will cause the AB cell to skew clockwise in the AP-DV plane (when viewed from the left side down the left-right axis), thereby establishing the dorsoventral axis.

claim: Integrin complexes have been shown to anchor the Tribolium blastoderm to the vitelline envelope.
source: Although a role for integrins has not been reported during early C. elegans development, integrin complexes have been shown to anchor the Tribolium blastoderm to the vitelline envelope (Münster et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature
